claims.text: Forming an aluminum oxide coating by pack cementation can improve the high-temperature oxygen resistance of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Pack cementation forms an aluminum oxide coating on the alloy.
The intervention should work at temperatures above 1000°C.
The intervention should work in an oxygen-rich atmosphere.
The intervention should remain effective for exposure times exceeding 100 hours.
The coating produces a dense, continuous aluminum oxide layer.
The aluminum oxide layer acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Suppressing oxygen diffusion reduces oxidation and degradation of the alloy.
The coated alloy will have an oxidation rate at least 50% lower than the untreated alloy.
The claimed operating boundary is 1000–1200°C, an oxygen-rich atmosphere, and 100–500 hours of exposure.
Coating effectiveness may depend on the composition of the refractory high-entropy alloy.
Coating effectiveness may depend on pack-cementation process parameters.
Failure of the coated alloy to exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate than the untreated alloy after 200 hours at 1100°C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions require temperatures above 1000°C and exposure exceeding 100 hours, whereas the stated boundary includes exactly 1000°C and exactly 100 hours.

The prediction requires at least a 50% oxidation-rate reduction, but the falsification rule only requires a statistically significant reduction. A significant reduction smaller than 50% would violate the prediction without falsifying the hypothesis under the stated rule.
